questions.prompt: Which rewrite of 'Our method significantly outperforms the baseline' is best supported by 5-seed data with a 1.8-point mean gain whose 95% interval is [-1.2, 4.8]?
options: Our method clearly outperforms the baseline, since the mean gain of 1.8 points is positive.
Our method scores 1.8 points higher on average (95% CI -1.2 to 4.8, n=5 seeds), within seed noise.
Our method is comparable to the baseline, so no numbers or intervals need to be reported.
Our method is slightly but significantly better, with a gain of 1.8 points over the baseline.
questions.explanation: The interval includes zero, so 'significantly' is unjustified; the honest sentence reports the number, the interval and n.

questions.prompt: Four runs scored 70, 74, 72, 76. What is the sample standard deviation (divide by n-1)? Give 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Mean 73, deviations -3, 1, -1, 3, sum of squares 20, variance 20/3, sd = 2.58.

questions.prompt: For the same four runs (70, 74, 72, 76), what is the half-width of the 95% confidence interval of the mean, using t = 3.182 for 3 degrees of freedom? Give 2 decimals.
A bar chart of two methods (71 and 72.8) uses a y-axis that starts at 70 and shows no error bars. What is the main problem?
options: Bars should always be replaced by pie charts, because they show proportions better.
The colours are not taken from a standard palette, so readers cannot compare them.
The chart is missing a title, so the reader cannot tell which metric it shows.
Bar heights no longer reflect the values, and without error bars a small gap looks large.
questions.explanation: Bars encode value by length, so a truncated axis exaggerates differences; showing the data points with intervals avoids this.

questions.prompt: A truncated bar chart starts its axis at 60 and shows bars for 62 and 65. What is the ratio of the bar heights (taller/shorter)?
questions.explanation: Heights are 2 and 5, ratio 2.5, while the true ratio of values is 65/62 = 1.05.

questions.prompt: A paper only tested a gripper in simulation. Write one specific limitation sentence and say how you would test it.
rubric: Names what was not tested (real friction, sensing, actuation) rather than vague 'more work needed'.
Says why it could change the conclusion.
Gives a concrete test (hardware trials, parameter sweep) with a measurable outcome.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: A result is written as '72.8 ± 1.9'. What must the text or caption add?
options: Nothing; plus-minus always means one standard deviation, so the reader can infer it.
Only the units of the measured quantity, since the interval convention is standard.
Whether 1.9 is a standard deviation, a standard error or a CI half-width, and what n is.
Only the colour and line style of the error bars drawn in the figure.
questions.explanation: Different conventions give very different widths. State which and give n.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would implement a check that flags vague claims in a results paragraph and what it cannot detect.
rubric: Splits into sentences and looks for vague words (significantly, robust, state-of-the-art) without a number in the same sentence.
Optionally checks for sample size and a limitation statement.
Admits it cannot judge whether the numbers are correct or the argument is sound.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
